shots.spoken: Your own crop needs work.
But some of your work is owed elsewhere.
In one English record from twelve seventy-nine, Hugh Miller's holding owed three days of labour each week, with some holiday weeks exempt.
In autumn, the requirement called for two workers.
His own fields still needed tending.
Apparently, the arrangement expected a spare Hugh. Disappointing news for anyone issued with only one Hugh.
So this isn't simply a life where you work hard and eat what you've grown.
You have to fit your household's needs around other claims on your time and produce.
Let's follow one possible life in a farming household in medieval England, starting in the late twelve hundreds.
Our scenes are reconstructed; the records are examples from different places.
Before you become the person expected to do the work, you're the child watching other people do it.
Picture a modest home with a hearth and a shared living space.
In this home, the room where you eat is also a place to sleep.
Around the household are places for animals and stored crops.
As a small child, you need feeding and looking after.
You can play too. Dolls and spinning tops belong in the medieval world;
childhood wasn't just adulthood with shorter legs.
For our first little scene, you're playing with a doll while someone prepares food.
Later, the same space has to serve another purpose.
Your toy moves out of the way; the household doesn't have a room for every activity.
As you grow, helping becomes part of your life.
Rural children could tend small animals, help in gardens or assist with food preparation.
Imagine someone showing you how to feed the chickens.
You watch, help,
and eventually do the task while that person turns to something else.
The chickens have acquired a new member of staff.
Their feedback is immediate and extremely loud.
Now another job can happen at the same time. What changes isn't just your ability to feed birds.
Somebody can rely on you, and the household can divide its work differently.
Those birds are part of the household's resources.
Later, we'll meet a holding where even chickens appear among the things owed to the lord. The animals you've learned to care for may have a job beyond being annoying.
Growing up around farming means getting to know work that changes as the crop changes.
Ground has to be prepared and seed sown.
Harvest is a different set of tasks. Let's stay with that part long enough to see what you're actually doing.
You cut the crop.
The cut stalks are still lying in the field.
Somebody gathers them into a bundle.
You lift it,
carry it to where it's being collected,
put it down and return.
One bundle has arrived.
The rest of the crop has not received the memo.
You give the next bundle your most exhausted look.
Nothing.
Back to carrying.
With another person gathering while you carry, you don't both have to stop for every step. You're doing different parts of the same job.
In our scene, the collection grows as more bundles arrive.
But having learned to work doesn't mean you can choose every task for yourself.
For your adult life, we're following the route of someone who has a holding with labour obligations.
Not everyone obtained the same land or had the same status.
You might do the work owed, then turn back to your household's crop.
Your hands haven't changed. Who the work is for has.
That's why finishing one job can leave another waiting. The field that feeds you still needs attention, even after you've supplied labour elsewhere.
Come home with part of the harvest.
Let's keep following the person who helped you carry it. Once home, they turn to preparing food.
You bring something to the table, then take your place beside them.
The person who took part of the load in the field now passes you food.
You take your place in a household whose work you've been sharing.
Put bread beside a cooked meal. Perhaps there's cheese if you have it.
Evidence from pots at West Cotton points to meat-and-vegetable stews and dairy foods, though that doesn't establish daily meat for everyone.
You take a mouthful.
Work has produced something useful, and you can enjoy the meal you've helped make possible.
But bringing the crop home doesn't mean you can eat the entire store.
In our scene, put aside grain for sowing. Keep food for later.
Then remember the claims attached to the holding.
Hugh's record included payments, grain, three hens and a rooster each year, and five eggs at Easter.
Even chickens have made it into the paperwork. Nobody consulted the chickens.
His lord was the abbot of Peterborough.
You didn't need a castle and a sword to have claims on somebody's work and produce.
You can see the distinction on the table and in the store: food you've eaten, supplies you've kept, and produce that may be owed elsewhere.
If you need more food now and use grain kept for sowing, that can help today's meal.
It also leaves you needing to replace that grain before sowing.
The pile cannot be in two places at once, however strongly you feel about it.
Suppose a cooking pot needs replacing. Its fragments are on the floor, and
planting them is unlikely to improve your pottery supply.
So a life supported by farming still involves dealing with other people.
Households traded and bought things; some also made goods for sale.
With equipment, ingredients and customers, bread-making is one possible activity.
Let's imagine a batch sold.
The customer takes the bread.
You receive money.
Before you put it towards the pot, you provide for what another batch would need.
What remains may help get the replacement.
The money has already found another job.
You were rather hoping it might pay for something and retire.
If the exchange works, the replacement comes into your home.
The fragments can be put aside, and you can return to a familiar task with a usable pot.
Then a bad year can change what those connections deliver.
Keep that ordinary scene in mind: work, exchange, food brought home.
Now compare it with the famine that began in thirteen fifteen.
This was a crisis, not an ordinary year repeated throughout our character's life.
A writer at the time described heavy rain preventing grain from ripening and making harvesting difficult.
Suppose your supplies fall short and you find paid work.
You earn money and go to buy food.
During the famine, wages could rise while grain prices rose faster.
More money could buy less grain.
You are chasing dinner. Dinner has picked up speed.
The routine looks familiar. The result doesn't:
what you can bring home may no longer cover the shortage.
In April thirteen sixteen, the king complained that some people with large grain stocks were holding them back from sale,
hoping for higher prices later.
From the buyer's side: there can be grain in a store and money in your hand, without grain offered for sale.
This is where “just work harder” stops being a complete answer.
The writer who described the rain also described people dying of hunger.
Knowing your work, and being willing to do it, couldn't guarantee enough food.
Suppose you look for a different life elsewhere.
Fold what you can carry into a bundle and lift it.
Your belongings can go with you.
The crop, the home and the people you know can't all be folded into the cloth.
And depending on your legal position, some obligations may follow you anyway.
An earlier court record allowed Walter Hull to live elsewhere after a payment, with other people guaranteeing his obligations.
His services remained owed.
New address. Unfortunately, the old claims knew how to find it.
People did move.
That record doesn't mean every peasant was forbidden to leave. It shows why changing location wasn't necessarily the same as being released from obligations.
Then think about your next meal.
If you have work or support waiting, leaving may offer a better chance.
Without it, getting away from this arrangement doesn't yet give you something to live on.
Look back at the field. It's a source of work and demands.
It may also be a source of food. Both can be true at once.
People also challenged demands and defended rights.
One court case gave Hugh Cross a favourable decision over a disputed bank and hedge.
A limited victory, but a right protected.
So people weren't simply unaware of their options. The options themselves had conditions, costs and possibilities.
Suppose you reach old age with a holding to transfer.
You may need another person to take over work you've been doing.
Some tenants arranged support in return for passing a holding to a successor.
Depending on the agreement, that could mean food or access to a small amount of land.
One agreement at Stanton in thirteen forty-one gives a concrete example. An ageing couple and their eventual successor were to live in the same house and share their goods.
He was taking on responsibilities on the holding, with the prospect of eventually becoming its tenant.
That's a separate recorded case, not the guaranteed ending of our story. It shows a way land and a household arrangement could help provide for later life.
Someone without those resources couldn't assume the same option.
Now picture our final scene. Somebody else brings a bundle in while you sit.
As a child, you needed looking after. As an adult, other people relied on your work.
In later life, the balance can change again.
The land that once meant tasks you had to perform can become something you use to negotiate support.
You learned skills, shared a home, dealt with obligations and other people, and made choices within circumstances you didn't fully control.
Peasants varied in wealth and freedom.
This was one reconstructed path through that world.
For tonight, let the chair take a turn.
Finally, something in the household that improves when you put your weight on it.

overlays.reason: Name the competing claim briefly; reserve the full diagram for its explanation
Locate the case; preserve the holiday qualification
Hold the worker requirement against the single farmer's own field
Pay off spare-Hugh joke without the unrelated dummy
Identify reconstruction once before the life story
Summarize the room reuse only after it is demonstrated
Connect different jobs to the crop cycle
Distinguish resources from legal status
Return to who receives the work, once across the pair
Keep the material evidence and its limit visible
Distinguish the seed reserve from food
Show the recorded quantities rather than a prose sentence
Identify the lord without a castle stereotype
Show the reserve being used for food
Hold the resulting shortfall without restarting the card
Make the next-batch allocation visible
Clearly label the crisis comparison, once
Compare directions without inventing measured ratios
Give the comparison the whole clause, not only its last words
Distinguish grain present from grain offered for sale
Contrast portable goods with support left behind
Keep this separate recorded case identifiable
Ask the practical support question only when narration reaches it
Show what the legal victory actually covered
Explain the exchange of tenancy and support
Locate the later-life agreement
Relate the successor's work to future tenancy
